extracted.intended_audience: EPA rulemaking stakeholders (regulated industry, public interest groups), environmental lawyers, policymakers, and public commenters on CAA rulemakings
extracted.subtask_short: CAA endangerment determination for greenhouse gases
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how EPA should determine whether greenhouse gases constitute an air pollutant that may be reasonably anticipated to endanger public health or welfare under CAA §202(a), including the legal and scientific standards and evidentiary approach the Administrator should use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of endangerment and standard-setting decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not conflate the endangerment determination (whether air pollution endangers public health or welfare) with the separate decision about what regulatory standards to set or whether those standards will be effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The endangerment analysis addresses whether there is a problem that needs attention; consideration of how effective future regulations will be in addressing that problem belongs to the standard-setting phase. Requiring EPA to project the effectiveness of potentially many future rulemakings would be unworkable and speculative (especially for long-term, global issues like climate change).

rubrics_metrics.name: Endangerment composed of two reciprocal elements: risk and severity
rubrics_metrics.description: Endangerment should be assessed by evaluating both (1) the likelihood or risk of harm occurring and (2) the severity of the harm if it were to occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Ethyl: 'composed of reciprocal elements of risk and harm'—a lesser risk of a great harm or a greater risk of lesser harm can both justify endangerment. Evaluate the relation between risk and harm on a case-by-case basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: No fixed minimum threshold of 'significant' or 'probable' risk required
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no statutory requirement that the risk of harm must reach a specific magnitude (e.g., 'significant' or 'probable') to establish endangerment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethyl and Reserve Mining indicate that magnitude of risk sufficient to justify regulation is inversely proportional to the severity of harm; courts did not adopt a single universal threshold. The combination of risk and severity must be judged in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precautionary nature of the endangerment standard — no proof of actual harm required
rubrics_metrics.description: The endangerment standard is precautionary: EPA need not show proof of actual harm or that harm is probable; findings may be based on significant risk coupled with severity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethyl rejected arguments requiring proof of actual or probable harm. EPA can act on precautionary grounds when the risk/severity combination warrants it, while still confining judgments to reasonable limits (de minimis certainty may not justify action).

rubrics_metrics.name: Case-by-case evaluation and reasonable limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a particular combination of risk and harm constitutes endangerment depends on the facts of each case and must be confined to reasonable limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts emphasize case-specific judgments; absolute certainty of a de minimis harm might not justify regulation. EPA should assess risk and severity in context rather than applying bright-line rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not require EPA to project future regulatory effectiveness before finding endangerment
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA is not obligated to show that potential future emissions control strategies will have a significant degree of harm reduction as a precondition for finding endangerment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflating endangerment with the anticipated success of future controls is unsupported by statute, precedent, or legislative history and would impose speculative burdens on EPA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation focused on the risk if no action is taken (exclude planned adaptation/mitigation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Endangerment analysis should evaluate risks to public health and welfare from the air pollution assuming EPA has not taken action to address it, i.e., not projecting societal adaptation or mitigation into the baseline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two approaches exist: (1) evaluate the pollution's impacts absent planned societal responses (preferred by EPA), or (2) project adaptation/mitigation and evaluate remaining risk. EPA interprets §202(a) to call for the first approach to separate problem identification from responses. Considering adaptation/mitigation would intertwine problem identification with political and social projections and greatly increase complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation and mitigation are outside the scope of endangerment determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Projections of how society will adapt or mitigate future risks generally should not be considered when determining whether air pollution endangers public health or welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adaptation and mitigation are potential responses to endangerment and belong to planning/standard-setting or policy phases. EPA may note where literature already includes assumptions about autonomous adaptation, but deliberate projection of societal/political actions is inappropriate for the endangerment test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory structure separates problem identification from regulatory responses
rubrics_metrics.description: The threshold inquiry (endangerment and cause-or-contribute) is distinct from subsequent discretionary standard-setting and cost/economic consideration provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory separation supports evaluating whether there is a health/welfare problem independently of how costly or feasible the regulatory remedies might be; those considerations are addressed in later statutory provisions governing standard setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of major assessment reports as primary scientific basis
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA should place primary and significant weight on major, recent synthesis and assessment reports (IPCC, USGCRP, NRC) when evaluating the scientific state of knowledge for the endangerment analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These assessments are comprehensive, cover the full emissions-to-harm chain, synthesize thousands of studies, and undergo extensive peer and government review—thus representing the consensus and the best available science. EPA participation in and reliance on these reports is appropriate; EPA is not required to replicate a wholesale independent assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighting of individual studies and treatment of newer literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual peer-reviewed studies not incorporated into major assessments receive limited weight and are reviewed mainly to determine if they would alter judgments based on the major assessments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA reviewed commenter-submitted studies to see whether they change conclusions; where appropriate, the TSD was updated. The default is to rely on the synthesis reports unless new material clearly warrants changing the assessment conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and responsiveness to public comments in the TSD
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA should document how public comments and new information were considered and reflected in the Technical Support Document (TSD) and Response to Comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA updated and revised the TSD in response to comments where warranted; the TSD and Response to Comments explain editorial and substantive changes and how they affect the findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'air pollutant' under the CAA
rubrics_metrics.description: "Any air pollution agent or combination of such agents, including any physical, chemical, biological, radioactive (including source material, special nuclear material, and byproduct material) substance or matter which is emitted into or otherwise enters the ambient air. Such term includes any precursors to the formation of any air pollutant, to the extent the Administrator has identified such precursor or precursors for the particular purpose for which the term 'air pollutant' is used." (CAA section 302(g))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a capacious definition; the Supreme Court held greenhouse gases fit within it (Massachusetts v. EPA). EPA should treat greenhouse gases as physical chemical substances emitted into ambient air.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and breadth of 'effects on welfare' under the CAA
rubrics_metrics.description: All language referring to effects on welfare 'includes, but is not limited to, effects on soils, water, crops, vegetation, man-made materials, animals, wildlife, weather, visibility, and climate, damage to and deterioration of property, and hazards to transportation, as well as effects on economic values and on personal comfort and well-being, whether caused by transformation, conversion, or combination with other air pollutants.' (CAA section 302(h))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The list is non-exhaustive and the terms are expansive; EPA may consider effects beyond the listed categories when evaluating welfare impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public health interpreted as 'the health of the public' with epidemiological metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Public health should be understood in its natural meaning—'the health of the public'—and EPA has historically considered morbidity (e.g., impairment of lung function, aggravation of respiratory and cardiovascular disease, other acute and chronic effects) and mortality when evaluating health impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use standard public-health metrics and epidemiological evidence (morbidity, mortality) in assessing whether air pollution endangers public health; past NAAQS analyses provide examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of broad temporal and sectoral scope of climate impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Endangerment analysis must consider a very wide range of risks and harms across sectors and over long timeframes, including current harms and risks of future harms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because greenhouse gas effects span multiple sectors and decades, EPA should base the Administrator's determination on the compelling body of scientific evidence covering present and projected impacts across society and the environment.
